title: How a derailleur drivetrain works
summary: Follow rider input from the crank through the chain and cassette, then change gears and see what the derailleur actually changes.

steps.title: Your legs turn the crank.
steps.body: Pedal force creates torque at the crank. The crankset rotates the front chainring, turning rider cadence into chain motion.
steps.keyFact: Cadence is crank revolutions per minute. It describes how fast you pedal, not how fast the bicycle is moving.

steps.title: The chain carries motion rearward.
steps.body: Each chain link engages the chainring teeth and carries that motion to a sprocket on the cassette. The chain is the mechanical connection between your crank and the rear wheel.
steps.keyFact: The chain's linear speed is the same on the upper and lower runs; the sprocket sizes determine rotational speed.

steps.title: Tooth counts set the ratio.
steps.body: With the 50-tooth demonstration chainring, a smaller rear sprocket makes the rear wheel rotate more times per crank revolution. A larger rear sprocket reduces that ratio.
steps.keyFact: Gear ratio = front chainring teeth ÷ rear sprocket teeth.

steps.title: The derailleur moves the chain sideways.
steps.body: A shift changes which cassette sprocket the chain engages. The rear derailleur guides that lateral move and maintains chain tension as the effective sprocket diameter changes.
steps.keyFact: The derailleur does not create the gear ratio; it moves the chain to the sprocket that creates it.

steps.title: Easy gear or high wheel speed.
steps.body: At the same cadence, a larger rear sprocket produces fewer wheel revolutions per crank revolution. That lowers kinematic speed but gives a mechanically easier gear for climbing or acceleration.
steps.keyFact: There is no universally best gear. The useful gear depends on speed, gradient, rider power and desired cadence.

quiz.question: At the same front chainring and cadence, which change makes the gear mechanically easier?

options.label: Move to a larger rear sprocket
Move to a smaller rear sprocket
Rear sprocket size makes no difference

quiz.explanation: A larger rear sprocket lowers the front-to-rear tooth ratio, so the wheel turns fewer times for each crank revolution.
